title: Act II, Scene II
focus: the murder and its first guilt

teacherSummary.text: Lady Macbeth waits, saying she would have killed Duncan herself had he not resembled her father as he slept. Macbeth returns from the murder with bloody hands, haunted that he could not say 'Amen' and that a voice cried 'Macbeth does murder sleep.' He has carried the daggers away; he refuses to return, so she takes them back and smears the grooms with blood. Knocking sounds at the gate; Macbeth says all great Neptune's ocean could not wash the blood from his hand, and wishes the knocking could wake Duncan.

context.history: The murder happens offstage; Shakespeare shows its aftermath rather than the act. Blood, sleep and hands become the play's key image clusters.

significance: The scene reverses positions: Macbeth falls apart and Lady Macbeth stays controlled ('A little water clears us of this deed'). Her line is a confident claim the play will put to the test.
discussionQuestions: Why do people often feel guilt most strongly right after doing something wrong?
Where does imagery appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with masculinity, power and violence?

anchorPassages.text:
I’ll go no more:
I am afraid to think what I have done;
Look on’t again I dare not.
Infirm of purpose!
Give me the daggers: the sleeping and the dead
Are but as pictures: ’tis the eye of childhood
That fears a painted devil. If he do bleed,
I’ll gild the faces of the grooms withal;
For it must seem their guilt.
Exit. Knocking within.
Whence is that knocking?
How is’t with me, when every noise appals me?
What hands are here? ha! they pluck out mine eyes.
Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood
Clean from my hand? No, this my hand will rather
The multitudinous seas incarnadine,
Making the green one red.

claimEvidenceReasoning.claim: The scene contrasts Macbeth's overwhelming guilt with Lady Macbeth's practical denial, a contrast the play will reverse.
claimEvidenceReasoning.evidence: A little water clears us of this deed
claimEvidenceReasoning.reasoning: He asks whether "all great Neptune's ocean" can wash his hands clean, while she says "A little water clears us of this deed," as if guilt washes off easily.

weDoAnswers: Hyperbole: an entire ocean cannot clean the blood. Lady Macbeth's "little water" is dramatic irony: she will try to wash her hands in her sleep.
analysis.weDoWords: “Great Neptune's ocean”, “blood” and “clean” stand out. Macbeth imagines the whole sea unable to wash one hand, so the hyperbole measures how large his guilt feels.
analysis.weDoQ2: The line shows guilt as a stain nothing can remove; Macbeth believes no water will make him clean, while his wife thinks a little will.

segments.script: Today's words: surfeited — overfed; here, drunk; nightgown — a dressing gown worn over night clothes; resembled — looked like; nourisher — something that feeds and sustains; watchers — people who stay awake. “surfeited”: Origin of “surfeit”: Anglo-Norman surfet. “resembled”: Origin of “resemble”: Anglo-Norman resembler.

words.sentence:
He is about it:
The doors are open; and the surfeited grooms
Do mock their charge with snores: I have drugg’d their possets,
That death and nature do contend about them,
Whether they live or die.

words.definition: a dressing gown worn over night clothes
words.sentence:
Get on your nightgown, lest occasion call us,
And show us to be watchers.

Had he not resembled
My father as he slept, I had done’t.

Macbeth does murder sleep,” the innocent sleep,
Sleep that knits up the ravell’d sleave of care,
The death of each day’s life, sore labour’s bath,
Balm of hurt minds, great nature’s second course,
Chief nourisher in life’s feast—

Get on your nightgown, lest occasion call us,
And show us to be watchers.

segments.script: The murder happens offstage; Shakespeare shows its aftermath rather than the act. Blood, sleep and hands become the play's key image clusters. The scene reverses positions: Macbeth falls apart and Lady Macbeth stays controlled ('A little water clears us of this deed'). Her line is a confident claim the play will put to the test. Dialogue: Short, broken lines between Macbeth and Lady Macbeth after the murder show panic. Imagery: Blood on hands; "Macbeth does murder sleep"; "all great Neptune's ocean." Characterization: Lady Macbeth's control ("A little water clears us of this deed") versus Macbeth's horror. Watch for the prophecies: The Witches' riddling prophecies: notice how each promise shapes what Macbeth hopes, fears and does next.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Methought I heard a voice cry “Sleep no more! / Macbeth does murder sleep” slowly and put it in my own words: After the murder, Macbeth says he heard a voice cry that Macbeth has murdered sleep. Next, craft. I notice "sleep" repeated, and personified as a victim. The strongest word is “murder”: Macbeth uses it of sleep itself, so he has killed peace of mind. Then, effect. What does the voice crying "Sleep no more!" mean? My answer: The voice crying "Sleep no more!" means that Macbeth's guilt will deny him rest, and the loss of sleep becomes his punishment.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Ask: What words in this line stand out, and what do they suggest? Expected student answer: “Great Neptune's ocean”, “blood” and “clean” stand out. Macbeth imagines the whole sea unable to wash one hand, so the hyperbole measures how large his guilt feels. Ask: How does this line connect to guilt and conscience? Expected student answer: The line shows guilt as a stain nothing can remove; Macbeth believes no water will make him clean, while his wife thinks a little will.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the scene for dialogue, imagery (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about the murder and its first guilt? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Act II, Scene II develops the idea of the murder and its first guilt. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and symbolism shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The scene contrasts Macbeth's overwhelming guilt with Lady Macbeth's practical denial, a contrast the play will reverse. When the text says “A little water clears us of this deed” (Act II, Scene II, line 729), it shows this directly. He asks whether "all great Neptune's ocean" can wash his hands clean, while she says "A little water clears us of this deed," as if guilt washes off easily.
